results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

26 of the 27 aligned units match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph in spec order (p01-p22, p24-p27); the two units marked two_ideas (Introduction ¶2, In Practice ¶3) state exactly the two-part controlling ideas p02 and p21 declare.

results.quote: Whether your account model qualifies depends on decisions made at onboarding
results.finding: p23's controlling idea has three context dependencies: country and release stage, whether the account model qualifies, and whether the platform's exposure per seller can absorb money being spent sooner. The draft lists only the first two (outline: 'country, release stage and account model'); the exposure dependency, which is what decided Larkfield's case, is missing from the 'Depends on context' list.

Introduction ¶2 (license covers the product, not the duties / no switch) is the declared two-part thesis of p02, and In Practice ¶3 (postpone / four conditions for revisiting) is a decision and the conditions that make it a plan, as p21 declares; both are one idea with its consequence. No other unit was marked two_ideas.

Every body unit ties to a supporting claim: products-and-license to S1/S2, issuing to S2, availability ¶1-¶2 and ¶4 to S4 and ¶3 to S3, the comparison to S1/S3/S4, the Larkfield scene and decision to S5; introduction and conclusion units are context, synthesis or hand-off.

Each quotation is followed by its point (e.g. 'Adyen is the lender', 'One company puts its own licenses behind three products; the other assembles each from partners'); each table is introduced or followed by what it shows (products table and Figure 1 by the product definitions, the requirements table by 'The default therefore applies...', the availability table by 'do not line up by country', the comparison and Larkfield tables by their lead-ins and the following paragraphs); Figures 1-3 carry explanatory captions.

All 24 declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries and pick up the declared known information, e.g. p02 contrast 'The card is not one more endpoint', products section 'The first question needs vocabulary', p09 'Neither arrangement takes the operating work off the platform', issuing section 'One of those duties is new in kind', p12 'The default therefore applies', p14 'Cards and financing were further along', p20 'What decided the matter was the refund', p25 'Seen from here, [[part-7]] described one decision four times', p27 'each mechanism was described for one payment at a time... [[part-8]] puts the same mechanisms under conditions no single payment shows'.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: A Card for Tuesday's Sales ¶2
results.quote: the sections below follow them in order
results.finding: Both readers found the declared prerequisite/problem-solution order and named the five questions as its organising principle, but the scene promises one section per question while questions 4 and 5 are answered in one paragraph of a section headed only by availability; both readers went looking for sections that do not exist. The spec's order is sound; the promise in the prose overstates it (e.g. 'the chapter answers them in order').

results.finding: 'which' can refer to the whole list or only to Canada; read as the whole list it contradicts the previous sentence. Both readers had to wait for 'Stripe's two Treasury pages differ on Canada' to resolve it.

results.quote: Stripe's Treasury page (n.d.) says the opposite about itself
results.finding: 'Treasury' first appears as a page name and is never identified as Stripe's name for the financial-account product, yet the key availability fact for Stripe accounts ('Treasury for platforms is in public preview...') depends on the reader making that link.

The introduction opens on a puzzling scenario with real amounts and times (€117.47 booked at 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, visible Thursday) and the product manager's question; none of the weak patterns applies.

The conclusion sorts what is established, what depends on context and the author's view, widens to a part-level synthesis with a course of action, and hands off; it does not open with 'in conclusion', end on a restated thesis or hold body evidence (the €84.00 case is the declared callback).

'A platform that picks its account model for the look of its onboarding has picked its loss exposure, its workload and the limit of its product plan with it' is stated by no single section, and the so-what is explicit: 'A platform that cannot do this carries a liability it has not measured, and a product that keeps, spends or lends seller money enlarges it.'

The conclusion returns to both callback targets: 'the card for Tuesday's sales is an authorization service, a fraud process and a larger exposure before it is a feature' and Mila's €84.00 refund, booked on Adyen against Studio Noord's balance account with Larkfield's liable balance account behind it.

The intro reader predicted all six sections in order (scene, products and licenses, issuing with the two-second window and default, November 2026 availability, side-by-side comparison, Larkfield's decision likely 'not yet') plus the close of Part 7, the documentation-based dated evidence and the sober tone. Open questions (why the refund matters, regulatory depth) are ones the body answers.

The reader lists per provider the stage per country (Stripe public preview UK, private US/EU; legacy v1 closed; Adyen in development), the licensed institution, the preconditions (Stripe: bear losses, requirements collection, no hosted dashboard; Adyen: enabled per balance platform, extra verification, Authentication SDK) and the duties taken on, and treats the answer as a 17 November 2026 snapshot to recheck. Matches expected.

The reader states the ~2-second window (2 s Stripe, 2,000 ms Adyen), that the configured default (approve or decline) decides every purchase during the outage, that the platform decided the outcome when it set the default, and that the endpoint needs its own availability target. Matches expected.

Every availability statement carries country and stage and a date: accounts 'public preview... UK', 'private preview... US, AU, and the EU', 'in development phase'; cards and financing tables 'as of 17 November 2026' with consumer/stablecoin cards, US line of credit and Adyen's invite-only and pilot financing labelled; nothing in preview, pilot or development is called available.

What to Take Away ¶4 synthesizes Part VII as one loss assignment seen across the model, verification, the split and this chapter's products, returns to Mila's €84.00 refund (Adyen balance account with Larkfield's liable balance account behind it; Stripe platform balance), and Questions to Ask ¶2 then hands off to Part VIII. The miscount of 'four' is recorded under flow_is_followable.
